catalog_quote: [p. 112] El proceso de elisión del morfema de tercera persona se está generalizando en algunas hablas y esto produce también un cambio en el patrón acentual común de la palabra quechua, el cual recae en la última sílaba. [p. 83] Algunos lectos de esta zona transicional tienden a la ausencia de realización nasal y en su lugar aparece un acento agudo25 como en maytá rinki 'adónde vas', imatá ruwachanki '¿qué estás haciendo?. También se observa la tendencia a la elisión de la nasal de tercera persona singular -n en final de palabra, observándose también, en este caso, el acento agudo como en chaqrata ruwá hinata ‘el trabaja la chacra así’. [fn. 25] Este proceso se observa en las hablas de la zona trancisional, no así en las hablas más alejadas como Antabamba, Andahuaylas y los distritos Cachora y Huanipaca en Abancay. new_statements.translation: The elision of the third-person morpheme is spreading in some local varieties, and this also produces a change in the common accentual pattern of the Quechua word, which [then] falls on the last syllable. [...] Some lects of this transitional zone tend to drop the nasal, and in its place an oxytone (final) accent appears, as in maytá rinki 'where are you going', imatá ruwachanki 'what are you doing?'. One also observes a tendency to elide the 3sg nasal -n word-finally, with final accent again in this case, as in chaqrata ruwá hinata 'he works the field like this'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source presupposes, but never states, the ordinary Quechua word-accent pattern (penultimate: every phonetic transcription in the thesis is so marked, e.g. [kúyay], [wáyta], [timína]); what it states first-hand for Apurímac is only the innovation: when a word-final nasal suffix (-n/-m evidential, 3sg -n) is dropped in the Pachachaca transition lects, the word surfaces with final (agudo) stress, i.e. stress stays on the vowel that was penultimate before the loss.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress arising from elision of word-final -n/-m (evidential -mi/-n allomorph, 3sg -n); fn. 25: this process is found in the transitional lects, not in the more distant ones (Antabamba, Andahuaylas, Cachora and Huanipaca in Abancay); also observed by the author in Paucartambo, Cusco.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in connected speech examples; no discussion of citation forms vs phrases, no acoustic data. The default position (penultimate) is only implicit here; an explicit first-hand rule for this variety would have to come from Gutiérrez Camacho 2006 or, at Cuzco-Collao level, Cusihuamán 1976/2001.
new_statements.identity_note: Eastern Apurímac Quechua (east2551; Glottolog dialects Abancay aban1243, Antabamba anta1256, Cotabambas cota1242) is a member of the Cuzco-Collao (Cuscan) group; most descriptive statements about its prosody exist only at the Cuzco-Collao level (Cusihuamán 1976/2001, Cusco Quechua cusc1236/quz). Carbajal Solís 2004 describes the Pachachaca-basin transition zone: his Abancay and Antabamba points fall under east2551, while his Aymaraes and Andahuaylas points are Chanka/transitional (Ayacucho Quechua ayac1239). The final-stress-after-nasal-loss observation is explicitly limited to the transitional lects near the river (fn. 25), not Antabamba.

sources.note: No explicit default-stress rule. Phonology chapters cover only segments (stops, laryngealised/aspirated series, lenition). pp. 80, 83 (fn.25) and 112 (sec. 4.4.2) say that loss of word-final nasal suffixes (-m/-n evidential, 3sg -n) in the Pachachaca transition lects yields an 'acento agudo' (final stress), described as a change to the 'patrón acentual común de la palabra quechua'; all phonetic transcriptions carry penultimate accent ([kúyay], [wáyta], [timína], [rápra]).

Otras excepciones a la regla de acentuación en la penúltima sílaba son /aˈɾi/ ‘sí’ (Rowe 1950) y la expresión /kanˈʧɑ/'; enclitics -yá, -chá, -puni with own accent.
